claim: Excess noise damages sensory hair cells, resulting in loss of synaptic connections with auditory nerves and, in some cases, hair-cell death.
source: Excess noise damages sensory hair cells, resulting in loss of synaptic connections with auditory nerves and, in some cases, hair-cell death.
evidence: This is a general statement about noise damage to hair cells, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The cellular mechanisms underlying mechanically induced hair-cell damage and subsequent repair are not completely understood.
source: The cellular mechanisms underlying mechanically induced hair-cell damage and subsequent repair are not completely understood.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Hair cells in neuromasts of larval zebrafish are structurally and functionally comparable to mammalian hair cells.
source: Hair cells in neuromasts of larval zebrafish are structurally and functionally comparable to mammalian hair cells but undergo robust regeneration following ototoxic damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field about zebrafish as a model system.

claim: Zebrafish hair cells undergo robust regeneration following ototoxic damage.
source: Hair cells in neuromasts of larval zebrafish are structurally and functionally comparable to mammalian hair cells but undergo robust regeneration following ototoxic damage.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about zebrafish regenerative capacity.

claim: Free swimming larvae exposed to strong water wave stimulus for 2 hr displayed mechanical injury to neuromasts, including afferent neurite retraction, damaged hair bundles, and reduced mechanotransduction.
source: Free swimming larvae exposed to strong water wave stimulus for 2 hr displayed mechanical injury to neuromasts, including afferent neurite retraction, damaged hair bundles, and reduced mechanotransduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synapse loss was observed in apparently intact exposed neuromasts.
source: Synapse loss was observed in apparently intact exposed neuromasts, and this loss was exacerbated by inhibiting glutamate uptake.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synapse loss was exacerbated by inhibiting glutamate uptake.
source: Synapse loss was observed in apparently intact exposed neuromasts, and this loss was exacerbated by inhibiting glutamate uptake.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TBOA treatment experiments.

claim: Mechanical damage elicited an inflammatory response and macrophage recruitment.
source: Mechanical damage also elicited an inflammatory response and macrophage recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of macrophage behavior after mechanical injury.

claim: Neuromast hair-cell morphology and mechanotransduction recovered within hours following exposure.
source: Remarkably, neuromast hair-cell morphology and mechanotransduction recovered within hours following exposure, suggesting severely damaged neuromasts undergo repair.
evidence: This is supported by time-course experimental data showing recovery.

claim: Severely damaged neuromasts undergo repair.
source: Remarkably, neuromast hair-cell morphology and mechanotransduction recovered within hours following exposure, suggesting severely damaged neuromasts undergo repair.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of recovery of morphology and function.

claim: Functional changes and synapse loss in mechanically damaged lateral-line neuromasts share key features of damage observed in noise-exposed mammalian ear.
source: Our results indicate functional changes and synapse loss in mechanically damaged lateral-line neuromasts that share key features of damage observed in noise-exposed mammalian ear.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental findings with known features of mammalian noise damage.

claim: Unlike the mammalian ear, mechanical damage to neuromasts is rapidly reversible.
source: Yet, unlike the mammalian ear, mechanical damage to neuromasts is rapidly reversible.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing recovery and comparison with mammalian systems.

claim: Hair cells transduce stimuli through deflection of stereocilia, which opens mechanically gated cation channels.
source: They transduce these stimuli through deflection of stereocilia, which opens mechanically gated cation channels (LeMasurier and Gillespie, 2005; Qiu and Müller, 2018) and drives subsequent transmission of sensory information via excitatory glutamatergic synapses (Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hair cells drive transmission of sensory information via excitatory glutamatergic synapses.
source: They transduce these stimuli through deflection of stereocilia, which opens mechanically gated cation channels (LeMasurier and Gillespie, 2005; Qiu and Müller, 2018) and drives subsequent transmission of sensory information via excitatory glutamatergic synapses (Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The degree of damage depends on the intensity and duration of the stimulus.
source: The degree of damage depends on the intensity and duration of the stimulus, with higher levels of traumatic noise producing structural damage to sensory epithelia, including hair cells (Cho et al., 2013; Nordmann et al., 2000; Slepecky, 1986) and lower levels leading to various pathologies, including damage to the hair-cell mechanotransduction complex/machinery and stereocilia (Gao et al., 1992; Husbands et al., 1999), misshapen hair cells (Bullen et al., 2019), synaptic terminal damage, neurite retraction, and hair-cell synapse loss (Fernandez et al., 2020; Henry and Mulroy, 1995; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Puel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Higher levels of traumatic noise produce structural damage to sensory epithelia, including hair cells.
source: The degree of damage depends on the intensity and duration of the stimulus, with higher levels of traumatic noise producing structural damage to sensory epithelia, including hair cells (Cho et al., 2013; Nordmann et al., 2000; Slepecky, 1986) and lower levels leading to various pathologies, including damage to the hair-cell mechanotransduction complex/machinery and stereocilia (Gao et al., 1992; Husbands et al., 1999), misshapen hair cells (Bullen et al., 2019), synaptic terminal damage, neurite retraction, and hair-cell synapse loss (Fernandez et al., 2020; Henry and Mulroy, 1995; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Puel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lower levels of noise lead to various pathologies, including damage to the hair-cell mechanotransduction complex/machinery and stereocilia, misshapen hair cells, synaptic terminal damage, neurite retraction, and hair-cell synapse loss.
source: The degree of damage depends on the intensity and duration of the stimulus, with higher levels of traumatic noise producing structural damage to sensory epithelia, including hair cells (Cho et al., 2013; Nordmann et al., 2000; Slepecky, 1986) and lower levels leading to various pathologies, including damage to the hair-cell mechanotransduction complex/machinery and stereocilia (Gao et al., 1992; Husbands et al., 1999), misshapen hair cells (Bullen et al., 2019), synaptic terminal damage, neurite retraction, and hair-cell synapse loss (Fernandez et al., 2020; Henry and Mulroy, 1995; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Puel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Excess noise initiates an inflammatory response.
source: In addition to directly damaging hair cells, excess noise also initiates an inflammatory response (Hirose et al., 2005; Kaur et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inflammation is mediated by macrophages, a class of leukocyte that responds to injury by clearing cellular debris and promoting tissue repair.
source: Such inflammation is mediated by macrophages, a class of leukocyte that responds to injury by clearing cellular debris and promoting tissue repair (Wynn and Vannella, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Hair cells show a partial capacity for repair of stereocilia and synaptic connections.
source: While hair cells show a partial capacity for repair of stereocilia and synaptic connections, some sub-lethal damage to hair cells is permanent.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Some sub-lethal damage to hair cells is permanent.
source: While hair cells show a partial capacity for repair of stereocilia and synaptic connections, some sub-lethal damage to hair cells is permanent.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: A subgroup of inner hair-cell synapses are permanently lost following noise exposure in the mammalian cochlea.
source: Numerous studies of the mammalian cochlea suggest that a subgroup of inner hair-cell synapses are permanently lost following noise exposure (Cho et al., 2013; Hickman et al., 2018; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity is likely the pathological event that initiates noise-induced hair-cell synapse loss.
source: Glutamate excitotoxicity is likely the pathological event that initiates noise-induced hair-cell synapse loss (Hu et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019; Puel et al., 1998), but the downstream cellular mechanisms are still undefined.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The downstream cellular mechanisms of noise-induced hair-cell synapse loss are still undefined.
source: Glutamate excitotoxicity is likely the pathological event that initiates noise-induced hair-cell synapse loss (Hu et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019; Puel et al., 1998), but the downstream cellular mechanisms are still undefined.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current understanding.

claim: The cellular mechanisms that promote hair-cell synapse recovery following damage-induced loss are not understood.
source: Further, the cellular mechanisms that promote hair-cell synapse recovery following damage-induced loss are also not understood.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current understanding.

claim: Zebrafish sensory hair cells are structurally and functionally homologous to mammalian hair cells.
source: Zebrafish sensory hair cells are structurally and functionally homologous to mammalian hair cells (Coffin et al., 2004; Kindt and Sheets, 2018; Sebe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Zebrafish hair cells are optically accessible in whole larvae within the lateral-line organs.
source: In contrast to other vertebrate model organisms, zebrafish hair cells are optically accessible in whole larvae within the lateral-line organs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about zebrafish as a model system.

claim: Lateral-line organs (neuromasts) contain clusters of ~14 hair cells each.
source: These sensory organs, called neuromasts, contain clusters of ~14 hair cells each and are distributed throughout the external surface of the fish to detect local water movements.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about zebrafish lateral line anatomy.

claim: Neuromasts are distributed throughout the external surface of the fish to detect local water movements.
source: These sensory organs, called neuromasts, contain clusters of ~14 hair cells each and are distributed throughout the external surface of the fish to detect local water movements.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about zebrafish lateral line function.

claim: Zebrafish can repair and regenerate damaged tissues, including lateral-line organs.
source: Zebrafish can repair and regenerate damaged tissues, including lateral-line organs (Kniss et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The frequency used for mechanical stimulation (60 Hz) is within the optimal upper frequency range of mechanical sensitivity of superficial posterior lateral-line neuromasts.
source: The frequency used for mechanical stimulation was selected and further verified (see Method Details) based on previous studies showing 60 Hz to be within the optimal upper frequency range of mechanical sensitivity of superficial posterior lateral-line neuromasts, which respond maximally between 10and 60 Hz, but a suboptimal frequency for hair cells of the anterior macula of the inner ear (Levi et al., 2015; Trapani and Nicolson, 2010; Weeg et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Superficial posterior lateral-line neuromasts respond maximally between 10 and 60 Hz.
source: The frequency used for mechanical stimulation was selected and further verified (see Method Details) based on previous studies showing 60 Hz to be within the optimal upper frequency range of mechanical sensitivity of superficial posterior lateral-line neuromasts, which respond maximally between 10and 60 Hz, but a suboptimal frequency for hair cells of the anterior macula of the inner ear (Levi et al., 2015; Trapani and Nicolson, 2010; Weeg et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 60 Hz is a suboptimal frequency for hair cells of the anterior macula of the inner ear.
source: The frequency used for mechanical stimulation was selected and further verified (see Method Details) based on previous studies showing 60 Hz to be within the optimal upper frequency range of mechanical sensitivity of superficial posterior lateral-line neuromasts, which respond maximally between 10and 60 Hz, but a suboptimal frequency for hair cells of the anterior macula of the inner ear (Levi et al., 2015; Trapani and Nicolson, 2010; Weeg et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dorsal-ventral displacement of a six-well dish at 60 Hz and acceleration of 40.3 m/s2 (±0.5 m/s2) created water flow and disturbance of the water surface that was strong enough to trigger 'fast start' escape responses.
source: Dorsal-ventral displacement of a six-well dish at 60 Hz and acceleration of 40.3 m/s2 (±0.5 m/s2) created water flow and disturbance of the water surface that was strong enough to trigger 'fast start' escape responses—a behavior mediated in part by zebrafish lateral-line organs to escape predation (Figure 1B inset) (McHenry et al., 2009; Nair et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous research on escape behavior.

claim: 'Fast start' escape responses are mediated in part by zebrafish lateral-line organs to escape predation.
source: Dorsal-ventral displacement of a six-well dish at 60 Hz and acceleration of 40.3 m/s2 (±0.5 m/s2) created water flow and disturbance of the water surface that was strong enough to trigger 'fast start' escape responses—a behavior mediated in part by zebrafish lateral-line organs to escape predation (Figure 1B inset) (McHenry et al., 2009; Nair et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 'Fast start' escape responses can be activated by stimulating hair cells of the lateral line and/or the posterior macula in the ear.
source: 'Fast start' escape responses can also be activated by stimulating hair cells of the lateral line and/or the posterior macula in the ear (Bhandiwad et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Low dose (3 µM) copper sulfate (CuSO4) for 1 hr specifically ablates lateral-line hair cells, but leaves hair cells of the ear intact.
source: To verify that the observed escape responses were mediated predominantly by flow sensed by lateral-line hair cells rather than hair cells of the macula, we exposed a group of larvae to low dose (3 µM) copper sulfate (CuSO4) for 1 hr to specifically ablate lateral-line hair cells, but leave hair cells of the ear intact (Olivari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: 'Fast start' responses occurred significantly less frequently in larvae with ablated lateral line organs than in siblings with intact lateral line.
source: When subjected to intense water flow, we found that 'fast start' responses—defined as a c-bend of the body occurring within 15 ms followed by a counter-bend (Burgess and Granato, 2007; McHenry et al., 2009)—occurred significantly less frequently in larvae with ablated lateral line organs than in siblings with intact lateral line (Figure 1C and E; avg. 'fast start' responses:: 0.4 ( ± 0.1)/s in lateral-line ablated vs 1.5 ( ± 0.1)/s in control; three trials,10 s per trial; **p = 0.0043).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Some CuSO4-treated fish were unable to escape the waves and were swept out of view.
source: Accordingly, some CuSO4-treated fish were unable to escape the waves and were swept out of view (Figure 1E; arrowheads; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The strong water wave generated by the apparatus is stimulating lateral-line hair cells and evoking a behaviorally relevant response.
source: These observations indicate that the strong water wave generated by our device is stimulating lateral-line hair cells and evoking a behaviorally relevant response.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of reduced escape responses in lateral-line ablated fish.

claim: Larvae were exposed to an initial 20 minutes of strong water wave stimulus followed by 10 min of rest, then 2 hr of continuous stimulus.
source: To induce mechanical damage to lateral line organs, larvae (10–15 per well) were exposed to an initial 20 minutes of strong water wave stimulus followed by 10 min of rest, then 2 hr of continuous stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 A).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: The 10-min break in exposure was introduced early on when establishing the stimulus duration because it appeared to enhance larval survival.
source: The 10-min break in exposure was introduced early on when establishing the stimulus duration because it appeared to enhance larval survival; it was therefore maintained throughout the study for consistency.
evidence: This explains a methodological choice based on observation.

claim: Exposed neuromast hair-cell morphology was categorized as 'normal' (radial hair-cell organization indistinguishable from control) or 'disrupted' (asymmetric organization with the hair-cell apical ends oriented posteriorly).
source: Exposed neuromast hair-cell morphology was categorized as 'normal' i.e. radial hair-cell organization indistinguishable from control or 'disrupted' i.e. asymmetric organization with the hair-cell apical ends oriented posteriorly.
evidence: This describes the classification system used in the study.

claim: Position of the neuromast along the tail was associated with vulnerability to disruption; L5 was more susceptible to disruption than L4, which was more susceptible to disruption than L3.
source: Position of the neuromast along the tail was also associated with vulnerability to disruption; we observed a gradient of damage in the pLL from rostral to caudal that is L5 was more susceptible to disruption than L4, which was more susceptible to disruption than L3 (Figure 2F; Repeated measure One-way ANOVA *p = 0.0386, **p = 0.0049, *** = 0.0004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Supporting cells underlying displaced hair cells also appear physically disrupted.
source: Note that SCs underlying displaced hair cells also appear physically disrupted (indicated by white arrows).
evidence: This is based on observation from images.

claim: Disrupted hair-cell morphology was place dependent, with neuromasts more frequently disrupted following sustained stimulus and when localized toward the posterior end of the tail.
source: Disrupted hair-cell morphology was place dependent, with neuromasts more frequently disrupted following sustained stimulus and when localized toward the posterior end of the tail (*p = 0.0386, **p = 0.0049, ***p = 0.0004)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: lhfpl5b mutants show a similar gradient of neuromast disruption following mechanical injury as WT siblings.
source: lhfpl5b mutants show a similar gradient of neuromast disruption following mechanical injury as WT siblings.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing mutants and wild-type siblings.

claim: Periodic stimulus causes less neuromast disruption than sustained exposure.
source: Immediately following sustained exposure, 46 % of exposed neuromasts showed a 'disrupted' phenotype, whereas following a periodic exposure only 17 % of the neuromasts appeared 'disrupted' (Unpaired t-test **p = 0.0034).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: No apparent damage was observed in hair-cell morphology in the ears of larvae exposed to sustained stimulus.
source: Additionally, we examined hair-cell morphology in the ears of larvae exposed to sustained stimulus and observed no apparent damage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating our overstimulation protocol produces mechanical damage specifically to lateral-line organs.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The overstimulation protocol produces mechanical damage specifically to lateral-line organs.
source: Additionally, we examined hair-cell morphology in the ears of larvae exposed to sustained stimulus and observed no apparent damage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating our overstimulation protocol produces mechanical damage specifically to lateral-line organs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ear hair cells were not damaged.

claim: lhfpl5b mutants have intact hair-cell function in the ear, but no mechanotransduction in hair cells of the lateral line.
source: To determine if hair-cell activity plays a key role in the displacement of neuromasts, we exposed lhfpl5b mutants—fish that have intact hair-cell function in the ear, but no mechanotransduction in hair cells of the lateral line—to sustained stimulation (Erickson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research characterizing the mutant.

claim: Comparable morphological disruption was observed in lhfpl5b mutant neuromasts lacking mechanotransduction.
source: We observed comparable morphological disruption of mutant neuromasts lacking mechanotransduction (Figure 2G), suggesting that displacement of lateral-line hair cells is due to physical damage from the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutant fish.

claim: Displacement of lateral-line hair cells is due to physical damage from the stimulus.
source: We observed comparable morphological disruption of mutant neuromasts lacking mechanotransduction (Figure 2G), suggesting that displacement of lateral-line hair cells is due to physical damage from the stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutants lacking mechanotransduction still show disruption.

claim: Adjacent supporting cells in neuromasts with disrupted hair-cell morphology appeared similarly displaced and elongated.
source: Further, we observed the adjacent supporting cells in neuromasts with disrupted hair-cell morphology appeared similarly displaced and elongated (Figure 2E 'disrupted'; white arrows), indicating that mechanical injury disrupts the structural integrity of the entire neuromast organ.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from images.

claim: Mechanical injury disrupts the structural integrity of the entire neuromast organ.
source: Further, we observed the adjacent supporting cells in neuromasts with disrupted hair-cell morphology appeared similarly displaced and elongated (Figure 2E 'disrupted'; white arrows), indicating that mechanical injury disrupts the structural integrity of the entire neuromast organ.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both hair cells and supporting cells are displaced.

claim: Moderate noise exposures can cause damage or loss of cochlear hair-cell synapses, including swelling and retraction of afferent nerve fibers.
source: Moderate noise exposures can cause damage or loss of cochlear hair-cell synapses, including swelling and retraction of afferent nerve fibers, while more extended and/or severe exposures lead to hair-cell loss.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about noise damage in the cochlea.

claim: More extended and/or severe exposures lead to hair-cell loss.
source: Moderate noise exposures can cause damage or loss of cochlear hair-cell synapses, including swelling and retraction of afferent nerve fibers, while more extended and/or severe exposures lead to hair-cell loss.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about noise damage in the cochlea.

claim: A reduction in the number of hair cells per neuromast was observed immediately following exposure.
source: We observed a reduction in the number of hair cells per neuromast immediately following exposure (Figure 3D and E; **Adj p = 0.0019; N = 13 trials) as well as a significant reduction in the percentage of hair cells per neuromast innervated by afferent neurons (Figure 3F and G; ****Adj p < 0.0001; N = 12 trials).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: A significant reduction in the percentage of hair cells per neuromast innervated by afferent neurons was observed immediately following exposure.
source: We observed a reduction in the number of hair cells per neuromast immediately following exposure (Figure 3D and E; **Adj p = 0.0019; N = 13 trials) as well as a significant reduction in the percentage of hair cells per neuromast innervated by afferent neurons (Figure 3F and G; ****Adj p < 0.0001; N = 12 trials).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Significant reduction in hair-cell number was observed specifically in 'disrupted' neuromasts, while 'normal' neuromast hair-cell number appeared comparable to control.
source: With hair-cell number, we observed significant loss specifically in 'disrupted' neuromasts, while 'normal' neuromast hair-cell number appeared comparable to control (Figure 3D and E; Adj p = 0.3859 normal, ****Adj p < 0.0001 disrupted).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: A significant number of hair cells lacked afferent innervation in stimulus exposed neuromasts with 'disrupted' morphology, but not 'normal' neuromasts.
source: With hair-cell afferent innervation we observed a similar trend that is, a significant number of hair cells lacked afferent innervation in stimulus exposed neuromasts with 'disrupted' morphology, but not 'normal' neuromasts (Figure 3F and G; Adj p = 0.7503 normal, ****Adj p < 0.0001 disrupted).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Hair cells contain electron-dense presynaptic specializations—called dense bodies or synaptic ribbons—apposing afferent PSDs which constitute afferent synaptic contacts.
source: Hair cells contain electron-dense presynaptic specializations—called dense bodies or synaptic ribbons—apposing afferent PSDs which constitute afferent synaptic contacts (Davies et al., 2001; Sheets et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the larval zebrafish lateral line, afferent nerve fibers innervate multiple hair cells per neuromast forming ~3–4 synaptic contacts per hair cell.
source: In the larval zebrafish lateral line, afferent nerve fibers innervate multiple hair cells per neuromast forming ~3–4 synaptic contacts per hair cell.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about zebrafish lateral line anatomy.

claim: Significant reduction in the number of intact synapses per hair cell was observed following sustained exposure.
source: We observed significant reduction in the number of intact synapses per hair cell following sustained exposure (Figure 4D and F; **Adj p = 0.0078).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of intact synapses per hair cell was observed in all exposed neuromasts, with significantly fewer synapses in 'normal' exposed neuromasts relative to control.
source: When we compared 'normal' and 'disrupted' neuromasts following exposure, we observed a loss of intact synapses per hair cell in all exposed neuromasts, with significantly fewer synapses in 'normal' exposed neuromasts relative to control (Figure 4E–F; **Adj p = 0.0043 normal, Adj p = 0.1207 disrupted).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Significant synapse loss was observed in the neuromasts of fish exposed to the less mechanically damaging 'periodic' stimulus.
source: Additionally, significant synapse loss was observed in the neuromasts of fish exposed to the less mechanically damaging 'periodic' stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 F').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Excess glutamate signaling may be a key factor driving inner hair-cell synapse loss following exposure to damaging noise.
source: Previous studies indicate that excess glutamate signaling may be a key factor driving inner hair-cell synapse loss following exposure to damaging noise (Chen et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A significantly greater degree of hair-cell synapse loss was observed in stimulated neuromasts with 'normal' morphology co-treated with TBOA than in stimulated neuromasts co-treated with drug carrier alone.
source: We observed a significantly greater degree of hair-cell synapse loss in stimulated neuromasts with 'normal' morphology co-treated with TBOA than in stimulated neuromasts co-treated with drug carrier alone (Figure 4E; Two-way ANOVA. *p < 0.0187), suggesting glutamate excitotoxicity contributes to hair-cell synapse loss observed in mechanically overstimulated neuromasts with intact morphology.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity contributes to hair-cell synapse loss observed in mechanically overstimulated neuromasts with intact morphology.
source: We observed a significantly greater degree of hair-cell synapse loss in stimulated neuromasts with 'normal' morphology co-treated with TBOA than in stimulated neuromasts co-treated with drug carrier alone (Figure 4E; Two-way ANOVA. *p < 0.0187), suggesting glutamate excitotoxicity contributes to hair-cell synapse loss observed in mechanically overstimulated neuromasts with intact morphology.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking glutamate uptake exacerbates synapse loss.

claim: Synaptic debris (synapses that appeared detached and suspended from their associated neurons) were rarely observed in unexposed neuromasts.
source: While we rarely observed synaptic debris in unexposed neuromasts, we observed a greater relative frequency of synaptic debris in neuromasts exposed to strong water wave stimulus (Figure 5C; One sample Wilcoxon test, p = 0.1250 (control), *p = 0.0313(normal), **p = 0.0039(disrupted)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and statistical analysis.

claim: A greater relative frequency of synaptic debris was observed in neuromasts exposed to strong water wave stimulus.
source: While we rarely observed synaptic debris in unexposed neuromasts, we observed a greater relative frequency of synaptic debris in neuromasts exposed to strong water wave stimulus (Figure 5C; One sample Wilcoxon test, p = 0.1250 (control), *p = 0.0313(normal), **p = 0.0039(disrupted)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and statistical analysis.

claim: Two distinct types of morphological damage to afferent synapses were observed in mechanically overstimulated neuromasts: loss of synapses within neuromasts that appear intact that is exacerbated when glutamate uptake is blocked and a higher incidence of synaptic debris that appear detached from afferent neurites in all exposed neuromasts.
source: Taken together, we observed two distinct types of morphological damage to afferent synapses in mechanically overstimulated neuromasts: loss of synapses within neuromasts that appear intact that is exacerbated when glutamate uptake is blocked and a higher incidence of synaptic debris that appear detached from afferent neurites in all exposed neuromasts.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: The inner ears of birds and mammals possess resident populations of macrophages.
source: The inner ears of birds and mammals possess resident populations of macrophages, and additional macrophages are recruited after acoustic trauma or ototoxic injury (Warchol, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Additional macrophages are recruited after acoustic trauma or ototoxic injury in the inner ears of birds and mammals.
source: The inner ears of birds and mammals possess resident populations of macrophages, and additional macrophages are recruited after acoustic trauma or ototoxic injury (Warchol, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A similar macrophage response occurs at lateral line neuromasts of larval zebrafish after neomycin ototoxicity.
source: A similar macrophage response occurs at lateral line neuromasts of larval zebrafish after neomycin ototoxicity (Warchol et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Macrophages migrate into neomycin-injured neuromasts and actively phagocytose the debris of dying hair cells.
source: Analysis of fixed specimens, as well as time-lapse imaging of living fish (e.g. Hirose et al., 2017), has demonstrated that macrophages migrate into neomycin-injured neuromasts and actively phagocytose the debris of dying hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: 1–2 macrophages were typically present within a 25 µm radius of each neuromast.
source: Consistent with earlier studies (Hirose et al., 2017), 1–2 macrophages were typically present within a 25 µm radius of each neuromast (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citation to previous research.

claim: In uninjured (control) fish, macrophages remained outside the sensory region of the neuromast and rarely contacted hair cells.
source: In uninjured (control) fish, those macrophages remained outside the sensory region of the neuromast and rarely contacted hair cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: At 2, 4, and 8 hr after sustained stimulus, increased macrophage-hair cell contacts were observed.
source: However, at 2, 4, and 8 hr after sustained stimulus, we observed increased macrophage-hair cell contacts (Figure 6D; *p = 0.024), as well as the presence of immunolabeled hair-cell debris within macrophage cytoplasm (suggestive of phagocytosis, Figures 6A and 4 h., arrow).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and statistical analysis.

claim: Immunolabeled hair-cell debris was present within macrophage cytoplasm, suggestive of phagocytosis.
source: However, at 2, 4, and 8 hr after sustained stimulus, we observed increased macrophage-hair cell contacts (Figure 6D; *p = 0.024), as well as the presence of immunolabeled hair-cell debris within macrophage cytoplasm (suggestive of phagocytosis, Figures 6A and 4 h., arrow).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Macrophage-hair cell contact and phagocytosis peaked at 2 hr after exposure.
source: Macrophage-hair cell contact and phagocytosis peaked at 2 hr after exposure (Figure 6E; **p = 0.0013 (2 h)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The numbers of macrophages within a 25 µm radius of each neuromast remained unchanged at all time points after exposure.
source: Notably, the numbers of macrophages within a 25 µm radius of each neuromast remained unchanged at all time points after exposure, suggesting that the inflammatory response was mediated by local macrophages and that mechanical injury did not recruit macrophages from distant locations (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The inflammatory response was mediated by local macrophages and mechanical injury did not recruit macrophages from distant locations.
source: Notably, the numbers of macrophages within a 25 µm radius of each neuromast remained unchanged at all time points after exposure, suggesting that the inflammatory response was mediated by local macrophages and that mechanical injury did not recruit macrophages from distant locations (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that macrophage numbers did not change.

claim: This pattern of injury-evoked macrophage behavior is qualitatively similar to the macrophage response observed in the mouse cochlea after acoustic trauma.
source: This pattern of injury-evoked macrophage behavior is qualitatively similar to the macrophage response observed in the mouse cochlea after acoustic trauma (Hirose et al., 2005; Kaur et al., 2019; Kaur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous research.

claim: A decrease in the percentage of neuromasts showing 'disrupted' morphology was observed 2 hr following exposure, relative to fish fixed immediately following exposure.
source: We observed a decrease in the percentage of neuromasts showing 'disrupted' morphology 2 hr following exposure, relative to fish fixed immediately following exposure (Figure 7A; 54 % disrupted (0 h) vs. 32 % disrupted (2 hr); N = 4 trials; ), suggesting that physical disruption of neuromast morphology following mechanical injury is rapidly reversible.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Physical disruption of neuromast morphology following mechanical injury is rapidly reversible.
source: We observed a decrease in the percentage of neuromasts showing 'disrupted' morphology 2 hr following exposure, relative to fish fixed immediately following exposure (Figure 7A; 54 % disrupted (0 h) vs. 32 % disrupted (2 hr); N = 4 trials; ), suggesting that physical disruption of neuromast morphology following mechanical injury is rapidly reversible.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of decreased disruption over time.

claim: The average hair-cell number per neuromast at 2 hr post-exposure appeared to recover.
source: Consistent with this observation, the average hair-cell number per neuromast at 2 hr post-exposure appeared to recover (Figure 7C; *Adj p = 0.0321 (0h disrupted), Adj p = 0.1875 (2h disrupted); N = 6 trials; ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Recovery of hair-cell number occurred within 2–4 hours and corresponded with macrophages infiltrating neuromasts and phagocytosing hair-cell debris.
source: Recovery of hair-cell number occurred within 2–4 hours (Figure 6A and B) and corresponded with macrophages infiltrating neuromasts and phagocytosing hair-cell debris (Figure 6A and E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations showing temporal correlation.

claim: A lesser degree of afferent fiber retraction was observed compared to immediately following exposure.
source: We also observed, compared to immediately following exposure, a lesser degree of afferent fiber retraction (Figure 7E; ****Adj p < 0.0001 (0h disrupted), **Adj p = 0.0016 (2h disrupted); N = 6 trials) indicating partial recovery of innervation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Partial recovery of innervation was indicated.
source: We also observed, compared to immediately following exposure, a lesser degree of afferent fiber retraction (Figure 7E; ****Adj p < 0.0001 (0h disrupted), **Adj p = 0.0016 (2h disrupted); N = 6 trials) indicating partial recovery of innervation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced fiber retraction.

claim: A recent study characterized zebrafish lateral-line hair-cell damage induced by exposure to ultrasonic waves and reported a delayed hair-cell death and synapse loss 48–72 hr following exposure.
source: A recent study characterized zebrafish lateral-line hair-cell damage induced by exposure to ultrasonic waves and reported a delayed hair-cell death and synapse loss 48–72 hr following exposure (Uribe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Most exposed neuromasts examined showed 'normal' HC morphology 48 hr following sustained stimulus exposure.
source: Most exposed neuromasts examined showed 'normal' HC morphology Figure 7B; with no significant difference in hair-cell number (Figure 7D; Adj p = 0.4443; N = 4 trials).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: No significant difference in hair-cell number was observed 48 hr following sustained stimulus exposure.
source: Most exposed neuromasts examined showed 'normal' HC morphology Figure 7B; with no significant difference in hair-cell number (Figure 7D; Adj p = 0.4443; N = 4 trials).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Hair-cell afferent innervation after 48 hr was comparable to control fish.
source: Hair-cell afferent innervation after 48 hr was comparable to control fish; even the few neuromasts that remained morphologically 'disrupted' were fully innervated (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Even the few neuromasts that remained morphologically 'disrupted' at 48 hr were fully innervated.
source: Hair-cell afferent innervation after 48 hr was comparable to control fish; even the few neuromasts that remained morphologically 'disrupted' were fully innervated (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Previous studies in mice and guinea pigs indicate moderate noise exposures modulate the size of synaptic components.
source: Previous studies in mice and guinea pigs indicate moderate noise exposures modulate the size of synaptic components (Kim et al., 2019; Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A moderate reduction in synaptic-ribbon size was observed following exposure; ribbon volumes were significantly reduced relative to controls following 2 hr recovery.
source: We observed a moderate reduction in synaptic-ribbon size following exposure; ribbon volumes were significantly reduced relative to controls following 2 hr recovery (Figure 8B; Kruskal-Wallis test *p = 0.0195; N = 3 trials), and this reduction was specific to 'disrupted' neuromasts (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction in ribbon size was specific to 'disrupted' neuromasts.
source: We observed a moderate reduction in synaptic-ribbon size following exposure; ribbon volumes were significantly reduced relative to controls following 2 hr recovery (Figure 8B; Kruskal-Wallis test *p = 0.0195; N = 3 trials), and this reduction was specific to 'disrupted' neuromasts (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Dramatic enlargement of PSDs was observed immediately and 2 hr following exposure.
source: While the changes in ribbon volume we observed were modest and delayed in onset, we saw dramatic enlargement of PSDs immediately and 2 hr following exposure (Figure 8D; Kruskal-Wallis test ****p < 0.0001; N = 3 trials).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Relative PSD volumes were significantly enlarged in all exposed neuromasts regardless of whether neuromast morphology was 'normal' or 'disrupted'.
source: In contrast to the observed reduction in ribbon size, relative PSD volumes were significantly enlarged in all exposed neuromasts regardless of whether neuromast morphology was 'normal' or 'disrupted' (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Enlarged PSDs are the predominant structural change in mechanically overstimulated neuromast hair-cell synapses.
source: These data reveal enlarged PSDs as the predominant structural change in mechanically overstimulated neuromast hair-cell synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PSD enlargement was more dramatic and widespread than ribbon changes.

claim: An additional consequence of excess noise exposure in the cochlea is damage to mechanosensitive hair bundles at the apical end of hair cells and, correspondingly, disruption of mechanotransduction.
source: An additional consequence of excess noise exposure in the cochlea is damage to mechanosensitive hair bundles at the apical end of hair cells and, correspondingly, disruption of mechanotransduction (Wagner and Shin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Larval zebrafish lateral-line hair cells each have a hair bundle consisting of a single kinocilium flanked by multiple rows of actin-rich stereocilia.
source: Larval zebrafish lateral-line hair cells each have a hair bundle consisting of a single kinocilium flanked by multiple rows of actin-rich stereocilia (Kindt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The frequency of neuromasts with apparently disrupted appearance increased the closer its position to the tail.
source: We found the caudal neuromasts to be more damaged than the ones positioned more rostrally: the frequency of neuromasts with apparently disrupted appearance increased the closer its position to the tail (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from SEM imaging.

claim: The neuromasts of the control fish carry a bundle of long (10–15 µm), uniformly shaped kinocilia.
source: The neuromasts of the control fish carry a bundle of long (10–15 µm), uniformly shaped kinocilia (Figure 9A–E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from SEM imaging.

claim: The neuromasts of the fish fixed immediately after sustained exposure often appear to carry much shorter kinocilia, which lack bundling and, in some cases, pointing to different directions.
source: In contrast, the neuromasts of the fish fixed immediately after sustained exposure often appear to carry much shorter kinocilia (Figure 9F–H, yellow arrows), which lack bundling and, in some cases, pointing to different directions (Figure 9G and H).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from SEM imaging.

claim: The apparent kinocilia length difference between control and overstimulated neuromasts suggests at least some kinocilia may undergo a catastrophic damage event at the time of stimulation, as their distal parts break off the hair cells.
source: The apparent kinocilia length difference between control and overstimulated neuromasts suggests at least some kinocilia may undergo a catastrophic damage event at the time of stimulation, as their distal parts break off the hair cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of shorter kinocilia in exposed neuromasts.

claim: Some kinocilia show 'swollen' proximal shafts closer to the cuticular plate of the cell, some of which extend into a thinner distal part while others appear to lack the distal part completely.
source: This is further supported by some examples of kinocilia with thicker, 'swollen' proximal shafts closer to the cuticular plate of the cell, some of which extend into a thinner distal part while others appear to lack the distal part completely (Figure 9I–K, yellow arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from SEM imaging.

claim: The average diameter of kinocilia at the level of the hair bundle (L2-5) was significantly larger than control.
source: Accordingly, the average diameter of kinocilia at the level of the hair bundle (L2-5) was significantly larger than control, with a few kinocilia showing dramatically thicker widths ~ 2 x greater than the thickest control (Figure 9L; ***p = 0.0007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: When measured ~3–5 µm above the bundle, the exposed neuromast kinocilia have a somewhat larger average diameter relative to control, but not as dramatic as observed at the base.
source: When measured ~3–5 µm above the bundle, the exposed neuromast kinocilia have a somewhat larger average diameter relative to control, but not as dramatic as observed at the base (Figure 9M; *p = 0.0243).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Signs of damaged bundle morphology were observed following overstimulation, as stereocilia bundles often appeared splayed, with gaps between the rows of stereocilia.
source: However, we observed signs of damaged bundle morphology following overstimulation, as they often appeared splayed, with gaps between the rows of stereocilia (Figure 9I–K).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from SEM imaging.

claim: A significant reduction in the relative intensity of FM1-43 was observed in all exposed neuromasts immediately following exposure.
source: We observed a significant reduction in the relative intensity of FM1-43 in all exposed neuromasts immediately following exposure (Figure 10 D and F; ****p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Average stereocilia length obtained from 3D interpolated confocal image stacks was not significantly altered.
source: While phalloidin labeling of stereocilia revealed what appeared to be tapered hair bundles in some exposed neuromasts (Figure 10B'; yellow arrows), average stereocilia length obtained from 3D interpolated confocal image stacks was not significantly altered (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: FM1-43FX uptake showed recovery within 30 min and fully recovered over several hours.
source: Remarkably, FM1-43FX uptake showed recovery within 30 min and fully recovered over several hours. (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing time-course of recovery.

claim: Following 4 hr, nearly all neuromasts exposed to strong wave stimulus showed 'normal' morphology and relative FM1-43X fluorescence that was comparable to control.
source: The degree of FM1-43FX fluorescence recovery following mechanical damage appeared to correspond with recovery of neuromast morphology; following 4 hr, nearly all neuromasts exposed to strong wave stimulus showed 'normal' morphology and relative FM1-43X fluorescence that was comparable to control (Figures 10D, F, 4h recovery).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: This observed timeline of morphological recovery coincides with macrophage recruitment and phagocytosis hair-cell debris peaking 2 hr post exposure followed by full recovery of hair-cell number between 2 and 4 hr post exposure.
source: This observed timeline of morphological recovery coincides with macrophage recruitment and phagocytosis hair-cell debris peaking 2 hr post exposure (Figure 6D and E) followed by full recovery of hair-cell number between 2 and 4 hr post exposure (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on temporal correlation of experimental observations.

claim: No difference in the number of EdU positive cells per neuromast was observed in control and mechanically overstimulated larvae.
source: Additionally, we quantified proliferating neuromast cells by treating control and mechanically overstimulated to 5-ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU) larvae for 4 hr following exposure and saw no difference in the number of EdU positive cells per neuromast in each condition (Figure 11A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Most damaged hair cells are repaired within mechanically injured neuromasts.
source: Cumulatively, these data support that most damaged hair cells are repaired within mechanically injured neuromasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations of recovery without increased proliferation.

claim: Mechanical damage to the zebrafish lateral line induced by strong water wave stimulus is observable immediately following exposure, is specific to the lateral-line organ, and appears to be rapidly repaired.
source: Mechanical damage to the zebrafish lateral line induced by strong water wave stimulus is observable immediately following exposure, is specific to the lateral-line organ, and appears to be rapidly repaired.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: A recently published noise damage protocol for larval zebrafish used ultrasonic transducers (40 kHz) to generate small, localized shock waves and reported delayed hair-cell death and modest synapse loss that was not apparent until 48 hr following exposure.
source: These observations contrast with a recently published noise damage protocol for larval zebrafish which used ultrasonic transducers (40 kHz) to generate small, localized shock waves (Uribe et al., 2018). They reported delayed hair-cell death and modest synapse loss that was not apparent until 48 hr following exposure, was not accompanied by decreased mechanotransduction, and was observed in the inner ear as well as the lateral-line organs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The damage observed in the Uribe et al. study was not accompanied by decreased mechanotransduction, and was observed in the inner ear as well as the lateral-line organs.
source: These observations contrast with a recently published noise damage protocol for larval zebrafish which used ultrasonic transducers (40 kHz) to generate small, localized shock waves (Uribe et al., 2018). They reported delayed hair-cell death and modest synapse loss that was not apparent until 48 hr following exposure, was not accompanied by decreased mechanotransduction, and was observed in the inner ear as well as the lateral-line organs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Features of the damage observed with the strong water wave stimulus protocol—reduced mechanotransduction, hair-cell synapse loss, and rapid inflammatory response—may correspond to sub-lethal noise-induced damage of hair-cell organs.
source: We propose features of the damage we observe with our stimulus protocol—reduced mechanotransduction, hair-cell synapse loss, and rapid inflammatory response—may correspond to sub-lethal noise-induced damage of hair-cell organs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: High frequencies (40 kHz) used in the Uribe et al. study are far outside those that are detected by lateral line neuromasts supporting that cavitation in the water medium is likely causing the observed damage.
source: Mechanical overstimulation in the Uribe et al., study was induced using ultrasonic (40 kHz) actuators. Such high frequencies are far outside those that are detected by lateral line neuromasts (Levi et al., 2015; Trapani and Nicolson, 2010) supporting that cavitation in the water medium is likely causing the observed damage.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with known frequency sensitivity and citation to previous research.

claim: The present method more closely resembles the techniques that are typically used to study noise damage in the mammalian cochlea, where high-intensity acoustic energy causes hair cell and synaptic injury in specific regions of the cochlea that are best-responsive to the frequency of the stimulus.
source: The present method more closely resembles the techniques that are typically used to study noise damage in the mammalian cochlea, where high-intensity acoustic energy causes hair cell and synaptic injury in specific regions of the cochlea that are best-responsive to the frequency of the stimulus.
evidence: This is based on comparison with established methods in the field.

claim: Synapse loss in hair cells exposed to strong wave stimulation is greater when glutamate uptake is blocked, suggesting a shared mechanism of glutamate excitotoxicity between noise-exposed mammalian ears and strong water wave stimulus exposed lateral-line organs.
source: This idea is further supported by the observation that synapse loss in hair cells exposed to strong wave stimulation is greater when glutamate uptake is blocked (Figure 4E), suggesting a shared mechanism of glutamate excitotoxicity between noise-exposed mammalian ears and strong water wave stimulus exposed lateral-line organs (Kim et al., 2019; Sebe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and comparison with previous research.

claim: lhfpl5b mutant neuromasts, which lack mechanotransduction specifically in lateral-line hair cells, were comparably vulnerable to physical disruption as their wild-type siblings.
source: One is that lhfpl5b mutant neuromasts, which lack mechanotransduction specifically in lateral-line hair cells, were comparably vulnerable to physical disruption as their wild-type siblings (Figure 2G; Erickson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Hair-cell activity during stimulation does not underly the physical displacement of hair cells observed following strong water wave stimulus.
source: This finding supports that hair-cell activity during stimulation does not underly the physical displacement of hair cells observed following strong water wave stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutants lacking mechanotransduction still show disruption.

claim: Physical disruption of the neuromast affects the whole organ—hair cells and their adjacent supporting cells.
source: Additionally, physical disruption of the neuromast affects the whole organ—hair cells and their adjacent supporting cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: In mammalian ears exposed to high intensity noise, mechanical injury to outer hair cells is localized to stereocilia disruption and gross displacement of hair cells is not found.
source: This observation contrasts with what is observed in mammalian ears exposed to high intensity noise, where mechanical injury to outer hair cells is localized to stereocilia disruption and gross displacement of hair cells is not found (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Displacement of hair cells in mechanically injured neuromasts may be due to loss of structural support from displaced supporting cells.
source: Speculatively, displacement of hair cells in mechanically injured neuromasts may be due to loss of structural support from displaced supporting cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: As the lateral-line organs are superficially localized on the surface of the skin, some of the intense mechanical tension applied across the tail is likely coupled to neuromasts leading to the physical displacement of a subset of exposed neuromasts.
source: As the lateral-line organs are superficially localized on the surface of the skin, some of the intense mechanical tension applied across the tail is likely coupled to neuromasts leading to the physical displacement of a subset of exposed neuromasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical location and experimental observations.

claim: Reduced FM1-43 uptake was observed in 'disrupted' neuromasts.
source: Finally, we observed reduced FM1-43 uptake in 'disrupted' neuromasts (Figure 10F) and measurable changes to kinocilia likely reflecting mechanical damage (Figure 9; Wagner and Shin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Measurable changes to kinocilia likely reflect mechanical damage.
source: Finally, we observed reduced FM1-43 uptake in 'disrupted' neuromasts (Figure 10F) and measurable changes to kinocilia likely reflecting mechanical damage (Figure 9; Wagner and Shin, 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations and citation to previous research.

claim: The evaluation of subtle and functionally relevant damage to hair-cell stereocilia, such as loss of tip links and damage to the actin core, is a significant challenge in zebrafish neuromasts due to their small size.
source: One notable limitation to using this model is that the evaluation of subtle and functionally relevant damage to hair-cell stereocilia, such as loss of tip links and damage to the actin core, is a significant challenge in zebrafish neuromasts due to their small size.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the model system.

claim: It is remarkable how rapidly mechanically disrupted lateral-line neuromasts regain normal morphology and FM1-43 uptake.
source: Nevertheless, it is remarkable how rapidly mechanically disrupted lateral-line neuromasts regain normal morphology and FM1-43 uptake (Figure 10).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The superficial lateral line's direct exposure to the environment may require more robust mechanisms for repair, unlike hair-cell organs of mammals which are encased in bone.
source: The superficial lateral line's direct exposure to the environment may require more robust mechanisms for repair, unlike hair-cell organs of mammals which are encased in bone.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on anatomical differences.

claim: Significant loss of hair-cell synapses was observed in neuromasts that were exposed to strong water wave stimulus but not mechanically disrupted.
source: In contrast to de-innervation and modest hair-cell loss that we observed in mechanically disrupted neuromasts, we saw significant loss of hair-cell synapses in neuromasts that were exposed to strong water wave stimulus but not mechanically disrupted i.e. 'normal' (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Loss of synapses in 'normal' exposed neuromasts was markedly more severe when synaptic glutamate clearance was inhibited, suggesting that synapse loss may reflect moderate hair-cell damage resulting from overstimulation of hair cells and excess glutamate accumulation.
source: First, loss of synapses in 'normal' exposed neuromasts was markedly more severe when synaptic glutamate clearance was inhibited (Figure 4G), suggesting that synapse loss may reflect moderate hair-cell damage resulting from overstimulation of hair cells and excess glutamate accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data.

claim: Involvement of glutamate signaling as a key mediator of noise-induced synapse loss has recently been reported in mice; loss of glutamate signaling prevents noise-induced synapse loss and pharmacologically blocking postsynaptic Ca2+ permeable AMPA receptors protects against cochlear hair-cell synapse loss from moderate noise exposure.
source: Involvement of glutamate signaling as a key mediator of noise-induced synapse loss has recently been reported in mice; loss of glutamate signaling prevents noise-induced synapse loss and pharmacologically blocking postsynaptic Ca2+ permeable AMPA receptors protects against cochlear hair-cell synapse loss from moderate noise exposure (Hu et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Synapse loss occurred in neuromasts that appeared to be fully innervated.
source: Second, synapse loss occurred in neuromasts that appeared to be fully innervated (Figures 3B and 4 B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Pharmacologically activating evolutionarily conserved Ca2+ permeable AMPARs has been shown to drive afferent terminal retraction in the zebrafish lateral line.
source: This observation was initially surprising given that pharmacologically activating evolutionarily conserved Ca2+ permeable AMPARs has been shown to drive afferent terminal retraction in the zebrafish lateral line (Sebe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Subtle damage to afferents in 'normal' exposed neuromasts may accompany synapse loss but not be apparent as loss of innervation, as single afferent processes innervate multiple hair cells of the same polarity within an individual neuromast.
source: We propose that subtle damage to afferents in 'normal' exposed neuromasts may accompany synapse loss but not be apparent as loss of innervation, as single afferent processes innervate multiple hair cells of the same polarity within an individual neuromast (Dow et al., 2018; Faucherre et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The relative frequency of synaptic debris (i.e. synaptic components that appear detached from afferent neurites) was higher in exposed neuromasts with 'normal' morphology relative to control.
source: This idea is further supported by our observation that the relative frequency of synaptic debris (i.e. synaptic components that appear detached from afferent neurites) was higher in exposed neuromasts with 'normal' morphology relative to control (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Synaptic debris observed in exposed neuromasts with 'normal' morphology may be the result of excitotoxic damage at synaptic terminals while synaptic debris observed in 'disrupted' neuromasts may reflect mechanical disruption of supporting cells and retraction of afferent innervation from a subset of hair cells.
source: We speculate that synaptic debris observed in exposed neuromasts with 'normal' morphology may be the result of excitotoxic damage at synaptic terminals (Sebe et al., 2017) while synaptic debris observed in 'disrupted' neuromasts may reflect mechanical disruption of supporting cells and retraction of afferent innervation from a subset of hair cells (Figure 3C and F).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observations.

claim: Studies in zebrafish and mice support that mitochondrial stress combined with excessive synaptic activity may also contribute to hair-cell synapse loss.
source: In addition, glutamate signaling may not be the only driver of synapse loss resulting from excess stimulation. Studies in zebrafish and mice support that mitochondrial stress combined with excessive synaptic activity may also contribute to hair-cell synapse loss (Wang et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prior studies of larval zebrafish have shown that macrophages reside near the borders of uninjured neuromasts and migrate into neuromasts after ototoxic injury.
source: Prior studies of larval zebrafish have shown that macrophages reside near the borders of uninjured neuromasts and migrate into neuromasts after ototoxic injury (Hirose et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Macrophages migrate into neuromasts within ~2 hr of mechanical injury, where they contact hair cells and, in some cases, engulf hair-cell debris.
source: We found that macrophages migrate into neuromasts within ~2 hr of mechanical injury, where they contact hair cells and, in some cases, engulf hair-cell debris.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The macrophage response after mechanical overstimulation is similar to that which occurs after ototoxic injury to neuromasts.
source: Although this macrophage response is similar to that which occurs after ototoxic injury to neuromasts (Carrillo et al., 2016; Hirose et al., 2017; Warchol et al., 2020), the extent of hair-cell loss after mechanical overstimulation is much less than the injury that occurs after ototoxicity.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous research.

claim: The extent of hair-cell loss after mechanical overstimulation is much less than the injury that occurs after ototoxicity.
source: Although this macrophage response is similar to that which occurs after ototoxic injury to neuromasts (Carrillo et al., 2016; Hirose et al., 2017; Warchol et al., 2020), the extent of hair-cell loss after mechanical overstimulation is much less than the injury that occurs after ototoxicity.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental observations.

claim: Macrophage entry was observed in 30–40% of exposed neuromasts, despite modest hair-cell loss.
source: We observed macrophage entry in 30–40% of exposed neuromasts, despite modest hair-cell loss (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: It is possible that the morphological changes characteristic of mechanically injured neuromasts are accompanied by the release of macrophage chemoattractants.
source: It is possible that the morphological changes characteristic of mechanically injured neuromasts are accompanied by the release of macrophage chemoattractants.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Studies of noise exposure to the mammalian cochlea indicate that high levels of synaptic activity (without accompanying hair-cell loss) can evoke macrophage migration to the synaptic region.
source: In addition, studies of noise exposure to the mammalian cochlea indicate that high levels of synaptic activity (without accompanying hair-cell loss) can evoke macrophage migration to the synaptic region (Kaur et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The signals responsible for macrophage recruitment remain to be identified.
source: In either case, the signals responsible for such recruitment remain to be identified.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current understanding.

claim: The observation that macrophages had internalized immunolabeled hair-cell material suggests that recruited macrophages engage in the phagocytosis of hair-cell debris.
source: The observation that macrophages had internalized immunolabeled hair-cell material further suggests that recruited macrophages engage in the phagocytosis of hair-cell debris, but it is not clear whether macrophages remove entire hair cells or target specific regions of cellular injury (e.g. synaptic debris; Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: It is not clear whether macrophages remove entire hair cells or target specific regions of cellular injury.
source: The observation that macrophages had internalized immunolabeled hair-cell material further suggests that recruited macrophages engage in the phagocytosis of hair-cell debris, but it is not clear whether macrophages remove entire hair cells or target specific regions of cellular injury (e.g. synaptic debris; Figure 5).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty in the interpretation.

claim: The macrophage response to mechanical injury of zebrafish lateral-line neurons is similar to that which occurs after noise injury to the mammalian cochlea.
source: In any case, our data indicate that the macrophage response to mechanical injury of zebrafish lateral-line neurons is similar to that which occurs after noise injury to the mammalian cochlea (Warchol, 2019) and suggests that zebrafish may be an advantageous model system in which to identify the signals that recruit macrophages to sites of excitotoxic injury.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous research.

claim: Zebrafish may be an advantageous model system in which to identify the signals that recruit macrophages to sites of excitotoxic injury.
source: In any case, our data indicate that the macrophage response to mechanical injury of zebrafish lateral-line neurons is similar to that which occurs after noise injury to the mammalian cochlea (Warchol, 2019) and suggests that zebrafish may be an advantageous model system in which to identify the signals that recruit macrophages to sites of excitotoxic injury.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings.

claim: Immediately following mechanical overstimulation, the most pronounced morphological change observed in hair-cell synapses was significantly enlarged PSDs.
source: Immediately following mechanical overstimulation, the most pronounced morphological change we observed in hair-cell synapses was significantly enlarged PSDs (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: PSD enlargement may be a consequence of reduced glutamate release from hair cells following sustained intense stimulation.
source: Speculatively, PSD enlargement may be a consequence of reduced glutamate release from hair cells following sustained intense stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Mice and zebrafish fish lacking hair-cell glutamatergic transmission have enlarged postsynaptic structures, indicating that glutamate may regulate postsynaptic size.
source: Mice and zebrafish fish lacking hair-cell glutamatergic transmission have enlarged postsynaptic structures (Kim et al., 2019; Sheets et al., 2012), indicating that glutamate may regulate postsynaptic size.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reduced glutamatergic transmission in mechanically overstimulated neuromasts may be a consequence of transiently impaired mechanotransduction.
source: While our data do not directly support this idea, we speculate that reduced glutamatergic transmission in mechanically overstimulated neuromasts may be a consequence of transiently impaired mechanotransduction (Figure 10B and D; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on experimental observations and citation to previous research.

claim: Cholinergic efferent feedback, which has been shown to hyperpolarize lateral-line hair cells, may reduce hair-cell excitability during sustained strong wave exposure to protect against excess glutamate release, excitotoxic damage, and synapse loss.
source: Alternatively, cholinergic efferent feedback, which has been shown to hyperpolarize lateral-line hair cells, may reduce hair-cell excitability during sustained strong wave exposure to protect against excess glutamate release, excitotoxic damage, and synapse loss (Carpaneto Freixas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on citation to previous research.

claim: Presynaptic ribbons were not similarly enlarged, but instead showed a modest reduction in size following mechanical injury.
source: Interestingly, presynaptic ribbons were not similarly enlarged, but instead showed a modest reduction in size following mechanical injury.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Functional imaging of zebrafish lateral line has shown that a subset of hair cells in each neuromast are synaptically silent, and these silent hair cells can become active following damage.
source: Functional imaging of zebrafish lateral line has shown that a subset of hair cells in each neuromast are synaptically silent, and these silent hair cells can become active following damage (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Ribbon size has been observed to correspond with synaptic activity.
source: As ribbon size has been observed to correspond with synaptic activity (Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996; Sheets et al., 2012), reduction in ribbon size may reflect recruitment of synaptically silent hair cells following mechanically induced damage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reduction in ribbon size may reflect recruitment of synaptically silent hair cells following mechanically induced damage.
source: As ribbon size has been observed to correspond with synaptic activity (Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996; Sheets et al., 2012), reduction in ribbon size may reflect recruitment of synaptically silent hair cells following mechanically induced damage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on previous research.

claim: Previous studies indicate mammalian cochlear hair cells have some capacity for repair following sub-lethal mechanical damage, including tip-link repair and regeneration of a subset of ribbons synapses.
source: Previous studies indicate mammalian cochlear hair cells have some capacity for repair following sub-lethal mechanical damage, including tip-link repair and regeneration of a subset of ribbons synapses (Indzhykulian et al., 2013; Jia et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2019).
